title: Hash addressing
description: Content-addressable storage names data by its hash: the address IS the content's fingerprint. Same bytes, same address — always, everywhere. This makes storage location-independent (fetch from any replica), implicitly deduplicated, and self-verifying (re-hash on read). The hash function is the system's identity: SHA-256 today, with agility to migrate tomorrow.
mechanism: address = H(content). Store: put(bytes) -> address. Fetch: get(address) -> bytes, verify H(bytes) == address. The verification is free integrity checking on every read.
algo: O(bytes) hash per store/fetch. Addresses are fixed-size regardless of content size.
demo:
import hashlib

store = {}

def put(data: bytes):
    addr = hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()
    store[addr] = data
    return addr

def get(addr):
    data = store[addr]
    assert hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest() == addr, 'CORRUPTION DETECTED'
    return data

a1 = put(b'hello world')
a2 = put(b'hello world')  # same bytes
print('same content -> same address:', a1 == a2, '(dedup is automatic)')
print('fetch verifies:', get(a1) == b'hello world', '(self-verifying on every read)')

title: Deduplication
description: Deduplication stores each unique chunk once: backups of 100 similar VMs share 95% of their blocks, so 100x the logical data fits in ~5x the space. Fixed-size chunking is simple; content-defined chunking (below) handles insertions. The dedup index (hash -> location) is the hot structure — it must be RAM-fast, because every write queries it.
mechanism: Chunk -> hash -> lookup in dedup index -> store only if new. Reference counts per chunk for deletion. Index in RAM/SSD; the classic scale challenge.
algo: O(chunks) hashes per write; index lookup O(1). Space = unique chunks only.

title: Merkle trees
description: Merkle trees hash data hierarchically: leaves hash the chunks, parents hash their children, the root summarizes everything. Two trees with equal roots hold equal data — verified in O(1). Differences are found by descending to the differing branches, so sync transfers only what changed. Git commits, blockchains, and anti-entropy all ride on this structure.
mechanism: Leaf = H(chunk); parent = H(left + right); root published/signed. Compare roots; on mismatch, compare children recursively; exchange only differing leaves.
algo: O(n) build; O(1) equality; O(diff * log n) to find differences.
demo:
import hashlib

def H(x):
    return hashlib.sha256(str(x).encode()).hexdigest()[:8]

def root(chunks):
    level = [H(c) for c in chunks]
    while len(level) > 1:
        level = [H(level[i] + level[i+1]) for i in range(0, len(level), 2)]
    return level[0]

a = ['c1', 'c2', 'c3', 'c4']
b = ['c1', 'c2', 'c3', 'c4-changed']
print('root A:', root(a))
print('root B:', root(b))
print('equal:', root(a) == root(b), '-> descend to find WHICH chunk differs, sync only it')

title: Git objects
description: Git is the most-used CAS on earth: blobs (file contents), trees (directories), commits, and tags — all addressed by SHA-1/SHA-256 of their content. Identical files across history store once. The object model is the lesson: a tiny set of content-addressed types composes into version control, and every higher structure (branches, remotes) is just pointers to hashes.
mechanism: blob = 'blob <len>\0' + content, hashed. tree lists (mode, name, hash). commit lists (tree, parents, message), hashed. Refs (branches) point to commit hashes.
algo: O(bytes) per object; dedup across all of history automatic.
demo:
import hashlib

def git_hash(kind, content: bytes):
    header = ('%s %d\0' % (kind, len(content))).encode()
    return hashlib.sha256(header + content).hexdigest()

blob1 = git_hash('blob', b'hello')
blob2 = git_hash('blob', b'hello')
print('same file twice -> same blob:', blob1 == blob2[:64] or blob1 == blob2)
tree = git_hash('tree', ('100644 hello.txt\0' + blob1).encode())
commit = git_hash('commit', ('tree %s\n\nfirst\n' % tree).encode())
print('tree:', tree[:12], '| commit:', commit[:12])
print('blobs+trees+commits: tiny CAS types compose into version control')

title: IPFS
description: IPFS is CAS for the network: files addressed by CID (multihash of content), chunked into a Merkle DAG, fetched from any peer holding the blocks via a DHT. Same file, same CID, everywhere — deduplication across the whole network. The tradeoff is availability: content exists only where someone pins it; unpinned data gets garbage collected.
mechanism: Chunk file (content-defined); build Merkle DAG; CID = multihash(root). DHT maps CID -> peers; fetch blocks from peers; verify each against the DAG. Pinning = 'keep this'.
algo: O(chunks) to add/fetch; DHT lookup O(log peers).
demo:
import hashlib

def cid(data: bytes):  # multihash: <code><len><hash>
    h = hashlib.sha256(data).digest()
    return '1220' + h.hex()  # 0x12=sha256, 0x20=32 bytes

# Merkle DAG: file -> chunks -> root CID
chunks = [b'chunk1-data', b'chunk2-data']
root = cid(b''.join(cid(c).encode() for c in chunks))
print('chunk CIDs:', [cid(c)[:16] + '...' for c in chunks])
print('root CID:', root[:16] + '...')
print('any peer with the blocks serves them; pinning = availability')

title: Content-defined chunking
description: Fixed-size chunking breaks dedup when bytes shift: inserting one byte at the start changes every chunk boundary. Content-defined chunking (Rabin fingerprints) cuts at data-dependent boundaries — a rolling hash hitting a pattern — so insertions only affect nearby chunks. Rest of the file dedups perfectly. Borg, restic, and IPFS all chunk this way.
mechanism: Rolling hash over a window; cut when hash % D == 0 (average chunk D bytes). Min/max bounds prevent pathological chunks. Boundaries depend on content, not position.
algo: O(n) rolling hash; expected chunk size D. Insertions disturb O(1) chunks.
demo:
# rolling hash cuts at content boundaries: insertion shifts only local chunks
def chunk(data: bytes, D=8):
    h, chunks, start = 0, [], 0
    for i, b in enumerate(data):
        h = (h * 31 + b) & 0xFFFF
        if h % D == 0 and i - start >= 4:
            chunks.append(data[start:i+1])
            start = i + 1
    chunks.append(data[start:])
    return chunks

a = b'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog. ' * 3
b = b'X' + a  # one byte inserted at the start
ca, cb = chunk(a), chunk(b)
print('chunks A: %d, chunks B: %d' % (len(ca), len(cb)))
print('identical chunks despite insertion: %d/%d (fixed-size would be 0)' %
      (len(set(ca) & set(cb)), len(ca)))

title: Garbage collection
description: CAS accumulates orphans — chunks no longer referenced by any root. Mark-and-sweep GC traces from the roots (pins, branches, live snapshots) and deletes the unreachable. The danger is deleting too eagerly: a root added concurrently with the sweep must not lose its chunks. Production collectors use generations or epoch-based reclamation to make 'unreachable' a safe statement.
mechanism: Mark from roots (pins, tags, live refs); sweep unmarked. Generational: new chunks collected aggressively, old rarely. Concurrent marking with snapshot isolation.
algo: O(chunks) trace; generational amortizes it. Safety from epochs, not speed.
demo:
# mark-and-sweep from roots (pins)
chunks = {'a': b'data-a', 'b': b'data-b', 'c': b'data-c', 'orphan': b'xx'}
roots = {'snapshot1': ['a', 'b'], 'pin': ['c']}  # live references

reachable = set()
for refs in roots.values():
    reachable.update(refs)
collected = [c for c in chunks if c not in reachable]
for c in collected:
    del chunks[c]
print('collected:', collected, '| kept:', sorted(chunks))
print('roots = pins + snapshots + branches: unreachable is safe to delete')

title: Integrity verification
description: CAS verifies integrity on every read by re-hashing — corruption is detected, not silently served. Background scrubbing re-reads all chunks periodically to catch bit rot before all replicas rot. Erasure coding or replication then repairs from healthy copies. The chain is: detect (hash), locate (which replica), repair (copy). Without CAS's self-verification, silent corruption propagates into backups.
mechanism: Read: re-hash and compare. Scrub: scheduled full re-reads. Repair: fetch from healthy replica / reconstruct from erasure shards. Alert on scrub errors — they predict drive failure.
algo: O(bytes) per verification; scrubbing amortized over the schedule.
demo:
import hashlib, random
random.seed(1)

store = {}
for i in range(100):
    data = ('chunk-%d' % i).encode()
    store[hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()] = bytearray(data)
# bit rot strikes one chunk
victim = list(store)[42]
store[victim][0] ^= 0xFF

def scrub():
    bad = [addr for addr, data in store.items()
           if hashlib.sha256(bytes(data)).hexdigest() != addr]
    return bad

bad = scrub()
print('scrub found %d corrupt chunk(s): %s...' % (len(bad), bad[0][:12] if bad else ''))
print('repair: fetch from a healthy replica / reconstruct from erasure shards')

title: Immutable snapshots
description: CAS makes snapshots trivial: a snapshot is just the root hash. Creating one is O(1) — no data copied, just a new pointer. Snapshots never change, so backups are consistent by construction, and retention is deleting root pointers (GC handles the chunks). Time-travel restores are fetching an old root. ZFS, Btrfs, and every CAS backup tool work this way.
mechanism: Snapshot = persist the root hash + metadata. Copy-on-write for subsequent changes (new chunks, new root). Restore = set current root to the snapshot's root.
algo: O(1) snapshot create; restore O(changed chunks).

title: Delta encoding
description: Delta encoding stores only the difference between similar chunks: instead of two full copies, keep one base plus a diff. Git packfiles do this for similar blobs; binary diff tools (xdelta, bsdiff) for executables. It composes with CAS — the delta itself is content-addressed. The tradeoff is reconstruction cost (apply the delta chain) versus space.
mechanism: Find similar base (by size/type or content hints); compute binary diff; store delta addressed by hash. Reconstruct by applying deltas in order. Limit chain length to bound read cost.
algo: Diff O(n) typical; reconstruction O(chain length * n).
demo:
# delta: store the diff, not the copy (toy: run-length of changes)
base = b'hello world, version one here'
new = b'hello world, version two here!'

def diff(a, b):  # list of (offset, new_bytes)
    return [(i, bytes([y])) for i, (x, y) in enumerate(zip(a, b)) if x != y] + \
           [(len(a), b[len(a):])] if len(b) > len(a) else [(i, bytes([y])) for i, (x, y) in enumerate(zip(a, b)) if x != y]

def apply(a, d):
    a = bytearray(a)
    for i, chunk in d:
        a[i:i+len(chunk)] = chunk
    return bytes(a)

d = diff(base, new)
print('base %d bytes -> delta %d entries' % (len(base), len(d)))
print('reconstruct ok:', apply(base, d) == new)
print('Git packfiles: same idea, similar blobs, delta chains bounded')

title: Erasure coding
description: Erasure coding stores data with redundancy mathematically: split into k data shards + m parity shards (Reed-Solomon); any k of the k+m reconstruct the data. It beats replication on efficiency (1.5x overhead vs 3x) at the cost of repair bandwidth and CPU. CAS pairs naturally — shards are content-addressed, so reconstruction is verifiable.
mechanism: Reed-Solomon over GF(2^8): parity = linear combinations of data shards. Lose any m shards, solve for them. Shard placement across failure domains.
algo: O(k*m) encode; decode O(k^2)-ish. 1.5x overhead typical (k=8, m=4).
demo:
# XOR parity (k=2,m=1): any 2 of 3 shards reconstruct (Reed-Solomon generalizes)
d1 = int('1010', 2); d2 = int('1100', 2)
p = d1 ^ d2  # parity shard
shards = {'d1': d1, 'd2': d2, 'p': p}
print('shards: d1=%s d2=%s parity=%s' % (bin(d1), bin(d2), bin(p)))
# lose d2: reconstruct from d1 + parity
del shards['d2']
recovered = shards['d1'] ^ shards['p']
print('lost d2; recovered: %s (any k of k+m suffice)' % bin(recovered))
print('real: Reed-Solomon k=8,m=4 -> 1.5x overhead vs 3x replication')

title: CAS APIs
description: CAS APIs are minimal by design: put(bytes) -> address, get(address) -> bytes, plus exists, delete (by policy), and pin. Everything else — versioning, directories, access control — layers on top. The API's simplicity is its strength: any client in any language implements it in an afternoon, and the content addressing makes caching trivial (immutable = cache forever).
mechanism: REST/gRPC: PUT /objects -> {cid}; GET /objects/{cid} -> bytes (immutable, cacheable forever); HEAD for exists; pin/unpin for GC roots. Auth at the edge, not in the addressing.
algo: O(1) API surface; immutable responses cache at every layer.
demo:
import hashlib

class CAS:
    def __init__(self):
        self.store, self.pins = {}, set()
    def put(self, data: bytes):  # PUT /objects
        cid = hashlib.sha256(data).hexdigest()
        self.store[cid] = data
        return cid
    def get(self, cid):          # GET /objects/{cid} (immutable: cache forever)
        return self.store[cid]
    def exists(self, cid):       # HEAD
        return cid in self.store
    def pin(self, cid):
        self.pins.add(cid)

cas = CAS()
cid = cas.put(b'important bytes')
cas.pin(cid)
print('put ->', cid[:16] + '...')
print('get ->', cas.get(cid))
print('exists:', cas.exists(cid), '| pinned:', cid in cas.pins)

title: Hash agility
description: Hash functions age — MD5 fell, SHA-1 fell, SHA-256 is current. Hash agility means the system can migrate: multihash prefixes identify the algorithm per address, new writes use the new hash, old data re-hashes lazily or on access. Git's SHA-1 to SHA-256 migration and IPFS's multihash are the case studies. Design for migration on day one; retrofitting is painful.
mechanism: Multihash: <algorithm id><length><digest>. New objects use the new algorithm; verification tries the recorded algorithm; background jobs re-hash old objects. Dual-write during transition.
algo: O(objects) background re-hash; new writes O(1) with the new function.
demo:
# multihash: the address says WHICH hash was used -> migration possible
import hashlib

def multihash(data, algo='sha256'):
    ids = {'sha1': '11', 'sha256': '12', 'sha512': '13'}
    h = hashlib.new(algo, data).digest()
    return ids[algo] + '%02x' % len(h) + h.hex()

old = multihash(b'data', 'sha1')     # legacy objects
new = multihash(b'data', 'sha256')   # new writes
print('old:', old[:20] + '...')
print('new:', new[:20] + '...')
print('verifier reads the prefix, uses the right function: migrate lazily, safely')

title: Audit trails in CAS
description: CAS gives auditability for free: the hash chain from root to chunk proves exactly what bytes existed at a snapshot. Signed roots (the maintainer signs the root hash) make the whole dataset verifiable by third parties — this is how software supply chains prove 'this is what we shipped'. Timestamps plus hashes make the audit trail tamper-evident.
mechanism: Sign the root hash per snapshot; publish signatures; verifiers re-hash the dataset and check the signature. Transparency logs (like Sigstore) publish the signatures publicly.
algo: O(1) signature per snapshot; verification O(dataset) re-hash.
demo:
import hashlib, hmac

KEY = b'audit-key'
# snapshot: root hash + HMAC signature (real: Ed25519)
chunks = [b'part1', b'part2']
root = hashlib.sha256(b''.join(hashlib.sha256(c).digest() for c in chunks)).hexdigest()
sig = hmac.new(KEY, root.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
print('root:', root[:16] + '...')
print('signature:', sig[:16] + '...')
# verifier: re-hash everything, check signature
ok = hmac.new(KEY, root.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest() == sig
print('third-party verification:', ok, '(proves exactly these bytes shipped)')

title: CAS over the network
description: Fetching CAS objects over the network is naturally efficient: verify each chunk on arrival (no trust needed in the peer), fetch from multiple peers in parallel (swarming), and cache aggressively (immutable = no invalidation). BitTorrent is CAS file sharing; IPFS generalizes it. The protocol is simple because the addressing does the hard work — identity, dedup, and integrity are all in the hash.
mechanism: Want-list of CIDs; fetch from any peers (DHT discovery); verify per chunk; parallel fetch; local cache. Untrusted peers are fine — verification is cryptographic.
algo: O(chunks) parallel fetch; verification O(chunk) each.
